sentences.text: The holotype skeleton of this giant bird is severely fractured, though crushing is limited except for the skull parts.
The preserved part of the ulna lacks any diagnostic features, and a partial claw bone found later associated with the holotype has not yet been described.

Distinctive anatomical traits include a quadrate bone with a quadratojugal socket positioned farther back and a mandibular articulation surface that extends more anterioventrally compared to Teratornis, a coracoid shaft that is laterally compressed near the humerus and features an anterior-glenoid facet that is nearly flat, and a humeral shaft that appears sigmoid or S-shaped when viewed from above.

Argentavis has the second-largest wingspan of any known flying bird, surpassed only by Pelagornis sandersi, while the living wandering albatross reaches upwards of 3.5 meters, which is significantly smaller than estimates for this ancient giant.
It is the heaviest known flying bird, with a weight of up to 70 to 72 kilograms, whereas early estimates for the body mass ranged from 80 kg to 120 kg depending on the year of the study.

Initial estimates varied wildly, with Campbell and Tonni initially estimating the wingspan between 6.5 and 7.5 meters, a 1983 study suggesting as high as 8.3 meters, and a 2010 study estimating the wing skeleton length at 1.83 meters, suggesting it likely had a smaller wingspan than previously thought unless it possessed significantly longer primary feathers.

The genus Argentavis was named by Campbell and Tonni in 1980, and the only known species of the genus is A. magnificens, which was described by Campbell and Tonni in 1980 after the first remains were discovered by Rosendo Pascual and Eduardo Tonni.
Among Teratornithidae, A. magnificens is the second-oldest species, older than all others except Taubatornis campbelli.

Estimates suggest a wing area of 8.11 m² and a wing loading of approximately 8.64 kg/m², indicating that Argentavis primarily flew by soaring and used flapping flight only for short durations, a capability supported by research on modern condors suggesting it could fly effectively in normal conditions despite spending little time flapping.

The bird had strong legs for a running start but relied on wind and vertical distance to flap its long wings effectively, especially for takeoff, and likely used thermal currents to stay aloft with a minimum flight speed estimated at 11 m/s or 40 km/h.
Argentavis likely laid one or two eggs weighing about 1 kg every two years, and due to its size and flight capability, adult birds rarely faced predation, dying mostly from old age or disease.

Territories likely covered over 500 km², and the birds may have flown north-south patterns to avoid adverse winds while searching for food, with brain morphology inferred from endocast reconstruction suggesting it was a scavenger or kleptoparasite living in open, sparsely vegetated areas.
Argentavis is classified as a member of the family Teratornithidae, and it belongs to the family Teratornithidae.

Argentavis lived during the Late Miocene epoch, specifically the Huayquerian age, from the Tortonian to the Zanclean stages, approximately 8 to 5 million years ago, and radioisotope dating of the Andalhualá Formation yielded ages of 6.02 and 6.68 million years ago.
Fossils of Argentavis have been found in central and northwestern Argentina.
